title: Mass carries

data.source: Ornstein and Uhlenbeck (1930); Kramers (1940); strong Markov property; cited from memory. Simulated inertial rotor (section IV form with a museum noise term), seeded.

prediction: With mass, the speed at the cut is what crosses: it explains the share (1 - e^-x)^2 / (2 (x - 1 + e^-x)) of the next duration, x = mean duration / M, within 0.03; the flat inertial rotor is the overdamped rotor with a coloured force of rate 1/M; and a seed that does not act on the motion adds nothing once the speed is known.
baseline: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck velocity process and the Markov property of (position, velocity). Decoy: share = exp(-x).
relation: special case of the standard theory of a damped particle; CRR as given is silent on what crosses with mass
status_line: CRR here is: silent. With mass the momentum crosses every cut, by the standard Markov property of a damped particle, and in the flat rotor mass is the same thing as a lasting force.
why: The measured shares follow the first-order formula, the two rotors agree, and an uncoupled seed predicts only until the speed is known. All of this is the classical theory of a damped particle under noise. Phoenix gives the inertial form as ASSUMPTION with no noise and no screening claim; the noise term here is a museum variant. Nothing in it is a test of CRR against the world. "Mass carries" is a theorem only in this sense: if the cut rule leaves the speed alone, the speed is part of the state. That is a modelling choice plus ordinary mechanics. CRR as given has no noise on the inertial rotor and does not say what a cut does to the speed. That the speed cannot be left out is shown by argument only on a level ring. With hills it rests on the numbers.
